# Semantic model {#sec-semantic-model}

[Normative]{.status}

The semantic model is the core of the framework.
It defines how information is described so that it means the same thing to every participant,
whatever transport carried it and whatever system produced or consumes it.

This chapter defines the *mechanism* — Things, identifiers, relationships, schemas and the rules for consistency.
The *content* — the actual terms for vessels, observations, vessel data and so on — is defined in the vocabularies (Part II).

## Things

Everything the framework describes is a **Thing**.

- Tangible Things: a vessel, a buoy, a whale, a piece of floating debris.
- Intangible Things: an observation, an area, a notice, a voyage record.
- The model describes itself in the same way: **relationships** and **schemas** are Things too.

Treating everything uniformly means the same mechanisms — identity, versioning, signing, exchange — work for all of it.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How is a collection of Things, such as "hazards in my area", identified and referred to, so that it can be monitored for new members (@sec-binding-json-ld)?
For a collection defined by an area: how is the scope of the area defined, and how does the collection follow a vessel whose area changes as it moves?
:::

## Identity

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-001}
**NCF-SEM-001** · *Draft*\
Every Thing MUST be identified by an IRI [@rfc3987].
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-002}
**NCF-SEM-002** · *Draft*\
A Thing's identifier MUST NOT change when the Thing is updated or when it is carried over a different transport.
:::

To ensure long term stability of identifiers, authorities should consider use of a persistent redirect service such as `w3id.org`.

An IRI is an opaque identifier [@webarch].
What a Thing is, who owns it, and which version of it a representation carries are stated in its representation, not read from its IRI.
An owner allocates IRIs as it chooses, and a path such as `/notices/` or `/versions/7` is a convenience of its own, with no meaning to anyone else.
Nor is a Thing's owner the holder of its IRI's domain, as an IRI under a redirect service such as `w3id.org` shows: the owner is stated in the Thing, and proved by its signature (@sec-data-owners).
An IRI's authority still has two roles, neither of them a meaning of the Thing: it locates the server from which the Thing is retrieved, as the IRI's scheme defines, and it divides identifiers among naming authorities (see Namespaces, below).

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-004}
**NCF-SEM-004** · *Draft*\
An application MUST NOT infer anything about a Thing from the components of its IRI, such as its authority or its path, beyond what the IRI's scheme defines for retrieving it.
:::

See [provisional decision 0021](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0021-opaque-iris.md).

### Namespaces

The primary namespacing mechanism is the authority component of resource IRIs. 

- For hierarchical IRIs, such as ones using the `https:` scheme, the authority component should be registered in the Internet Domain Naming System.
- For URNs, authority is assigned by the namespace owner registered with [IANA](https://www.iana.org/assignments/urn-namespaces).

**Maritime Resource Names** (MRNs, `urn:mrn:…`) [@iala-r1023], used by the Maritime Connectivity Platform and Smart Shipping initiatives, provide a method for identifying maritime organizations and their resources within a subset of this framework.

## Relationships {#sec-relationships}

Everything is connected.
A relationship has at least a **from**, a **to** and a **type** —
for example *this observation* — *was made by* — *this vessel*.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-003}
**NCF-SEM-003** · *Draft*\
A relationship MUST identify the Thing it is from, the Thing it is to, and its type, each by IRI.
:::

Usually a relationship is a property of the Thing it is from: the property is its type, and its value the IRI of the Thing it is to.
It is then part of that Thing, stated by the Thing's owner and changed only by its origin, with the Thing's versions (@sec-origins).

A relationship with properties of its own is a Thing of its own: one with an owner other than the owner of the Thing it is from, a period during which it holds, or a signature of its own.
A charter, a crew member's service on a voyage, and a device's link to a responsible party (@sec-responsible-parties) are relationships of this kind.
Its owner, who may be neither of the Things it relates, such as a registry, states it.
Its period is its validity (@sec-validity), and its earlier versions (@sec-versions) tell a receiver which relationships held when data was produced.
Because such relationships are Things, they can be signed, versioned and exchanged like anything else.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-005}
**NCF-SEM-005** · *Draft*\
A relationship that has an owner, a period or a signature of its own SHOULD be a Thing of its own.
:::

A relationship stated by one party binds no one else: a device's owner can state that a vessel is responsible for the device, but the vessel has not agreed.
A relationship that binds both of the Things it relates, such as a responsible party's acceptance of responsibility for a device, or a charter, is **contractual**,
and holds only when the owners of both have signed it, or one owner when both Things have the same owner.
Each owner adds a proof of its own, and together they form a proof set (@sec-trust-security).

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-006}
**NCF-SEM-006** · *Draft*\
A receiver MUST NOT treat a contractual relationship as holding unless the owners of both of the Things it relates have signed it.
:::

A relationship is stated once, by the Thing it is from or as a Thing of its own.
The Thing it is to need not state the inverse: an organism need not list the sightings of it.
Finding the relationships that point to a Thing is a query over other owners' Things, for a service that indexes them, and not part of the model.

See [provisional decision 0023](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0023-relationships.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="To be written"}
Relationships for data ownership and responsibility.
For example, an observer works for a research organization, on a field trip sponsored by an agency; a crew member serves on a vessel, on a voyage.
A field trip and a voyage are alike: each is a period of activity that relates persons, organizations and vessels to the data produced during it.
These relationships extend the responsible parties of devices (@sec-responsible-parties).
:::

## Schemas and meaning

The meaning of a Thing is given by its **schema**, and schemas are themselves Things.
This is what makes the framework a living one: meaning can be defined, extended and redefined
without changing the framework itself.

Schemas are grouped into vocabularies (Part II), which reuse established vocabularies where applicable.
As different communities describe the same thing from different **perspectives** — a biologist and a navigator describe a whale sighting differently — the model supports **mapping between vocabularies**.

::: {.callout-warning title="To be written"}
Schema definition language; versioning and evolution of schemas; how mappings between vocabularies are expressed.
:::

Core vocabularies defined or referenced in Part II include:

- Time
- Quantitative Value, including Systems of Units
- Geometry, including Position and Shape
- Identity, including Person and Organization
- Creative Work, including Report and Notice with Revision History

## Rights and usage {#sec-rights}

The framework's vocabularies are public domain (see Part II), but that says nothing about the **information** described with them.
A sighting, a hazard report or a vessel's recorded data belongs to whoever published it, on terms they choose.
A government agency may publish openly; a commercial service may attach conditions.
Receivers need to be able to tell which applies.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-020}
**NCF-SEM-020** · *Draft*\
It MUST be possible for a publisher to state the license or usage terms that apply to any Thing.
:::

The terms are stated with `dcterms:license` [@dcmi-terms], whose value is the IRI of a license, such as a Creative Commons license.
Where the terms are the owner's own, the license is an ODRL policy [@odrl-model], which can state permissions, prohibitions and duties in a form a receiver can read, such as use for navigation only, or deletion after a period.
`dcterms:rightsHolder` names who holds the rights, and `dcterms:rights` can add a statement for people.

The terms belong to a version (@sec-versions): the owner states them in the Thing, they are signed with it, and they can change from one version to the next.
A copy carries the terms of the version it holds.
Whether a change of terms affects copies already made is for the terms to say.

A Thing need not state terms of its own.
One that does not takes them from the Thing it is part of, such as an occurrence from its event, or a record from its dataset with `dcterms:isPartOf`, and failing that from the default terms its owner publishes.
A receiver that finds no terms by any of these means knows of no license, and does not assume that the Thing is free to use.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-021}
**NCF-SEM-021** · *Draft*\
A Thing that states no terms of its own MUST be governed by the terms of the Thing it is part of, and failing that by its owner's default terms.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-022}
**NCF-SEM-022** · *Draft*\
A receiver that finds no terms for a Thing MUST NOT assume that the Thing is free to use.
:::

A Thing derived from others names their versions ([NCF-TRU-005](trust-security.qmd#ncf-tru-005)), so its terms can be checked against theirs, for example against an input's requirement to share alike.
Whether the terms are compatible is the responsibility of whoever derives the Thing, not of the framework.

A transport that cannot carry terms, such as AIS or NMEA 2000, loses them, and the receiver's copy is incomplete ([NCF-SEM-012](#ncf-sem-012)).
A receiver that needs the terms fetches the Thing by its IRI; it does not take a broadcast to be free to use.

Usage terms say what a holder may do with a copy of a Thing.
Who may read or change the Thing at all is a different matter, set by the authorization policy of its origin (@sec-identity-authorization).

See [provisional decision 0026](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0026-rights-and-usage.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Which ODRL actions and constraints does the framework need, such as use for navigation only, and does it define an ODRL profile for them?
How does an owner publish its default terms, and how does a receiver find them?
:::

## Changes {#sec-changes}

A Thing changes in one of three ways:

Create
: A Thing now exists, under a new identifier.

Update
: A Thing is modified, and keeps its identifier ([NCF-SEM-002](#ncf-sem-002)).
  Withdrawing or cancelling a Thing is an update: the Thing still exists, and says that it has been withdrawn or cancelled.

Delete
: A Thing is removed, and its identifier no longer identifies anything.
  Whether the identifier may later identify another Thing is for the authority that assigns it.

### Origins and cached representations {#sec-origins}

A Thing has one owner, and its changes are applied only by its **origin**: the server, or servers, that hold the Thing for its owner, not as a proxy or a cache.
An origin can be split across several servers: between a vessel and its shadow ashore (@sec-architecture), among servers on board, or among servers ashore, such as in several regions of a cloud.
The servers of a split origin are together responsible for the Thing's consistency, as the replicas of a replicated database are.
While they cannot reach one another, each may serve, and if it chooses accept, changes of its own, so that participants on either side see a different branch of the Thing's versions; once they can, they merge the branches into one current version (@sec-versions).
How they keep consistent is for them: an origin that accepts changes to a Thing at only one server at a time never branches, and one that accepts them anywhere merges.

Every other copy of a Thing is a **cached representation**, such as a vessel's copy of an authority's notice, or a chartplotter's copy of a sighting.
A cached representation changes only with changes from the origin, attributed to the Thing's owner by a signature or by trust in the transport that carried them (@sec-trust-security).

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-031}
**NCF-SEM-031** · *Draft*\
A change to a Thing MUST be applied only by the Thing's origin; every other copy of the Thing is a cached representation.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-032}
**NCF-SEM-032** · *Draft*\
The servers of a split origin MUST merge every branch of a Thing's versions, so that they come to agree on one current version.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-033}
**NCF-SEM-033** · *Draft*\
A participant MUST NOT update a cached representation of a Thing with a change that it cannot attribute to the Thing's owner.
:::

### Scheduled changes

A change can be **scheduled**: given in advance, with the time at which it takes effect.
Expiry is a scheduled update: a notice that expires at a stated time says, in effect, "unless you hear otherwise, apply this update then" (@sec-vocab-notices).
A create is never scheduled.
A Thing that comes into force later is created at once, with a scheduled update that brings it into force, so that the date it comes into force can itself be changed.

A scheduled change names the version of the Thing it was scheduled against (@sec-versions).
At its time, the origin, and every participant that holds a cached representation, applies it if the Thing is still at that version, and discards it otherwise.
Any change to the Thing therefore cancels the changes scheduled against its earlier version, so that no scheduled change takes effect on a Thing its owner has since revised.
An owner that revises a Thing restates, in the same change, every scheduled change it means to keep.
A schedule held within the Thing, such as the end of a notice's validity, is restated by every update.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-030}
**NCF-SEM-030** · *Draft*\
At the time a scheduled change to a Thing states, the Thing's origin, and every participant that holds a cached representation of the Thing, MUST apply the change if the Thing is still at the version the change was scheduled against, and MUST discard the change otherwise.
:::

A scheduled change is held within the Thing, or in another container that the Thing references, such as a work queue; either way a receiver reaches it from the Thing.
Over a transport that cannot carry references, a scheduled change travels within the message, as the duration of an AIS Area Notice does (@sec-binding-ais).

Because a scheduled change needs no further message, a participant applies it to a cached representation even when it has lost contact with the Thing's origin.
Applying it gives the Thing a new version, the one the change names ([NCF-SEM-042](#ncf-sem-042)), so the copy is still a cached representation of the origin's Thing, refreshed as the owner directed.
Copies that apply the change independently reach that version eventually, not at one instant: copies of a Thing are not required to agree at every moment, since some are held by participants that are offline.

The time of a scheduled change is in UTC.
A participant without a synchronized clock judges the time as best it can, and records in the provenance of its copy (@sec-trust-security) that it applied the change by an unsynchronized clock.

### Validity {#sec-validity}

A value's **validity** is how long it holds in the world: a heading for a few seconds, an AIS target until it is lost, a notice for its period of validity.
Validity belongs to the Thing.
It is distinct from cache freshness, how long a cached representation may be used before it is checked with the origin, which each binding defines for its transports (Part III), as HTTP does with `Cache-Control` [@rfc9111].
A binding may derive a cache's freshness from the Thing's next scheduled change.

Validity is expressed as a scheduled update that marks the value as no longer current: "unless you hear otherwise, this value is stale at this time".
Each update that gives a new value restates it with a later time, so a value that is updated regularly never lapses, and one whose updates stop lapses at its time,
at the origin and at every cached representation, whether or not they are in contact.
A value that lapses keeps its last value, marked as no longer current, and the Thing is not deleted: an AIS target that is lost, for example, remains at its IRI, marked as lost.

A value whose validity differs from the rest of a Thing's, such as a vessel's position beside its name, is a Thing of its own, to which the vessel refers (@sec-relationships).
It then has its own versions and its own validity, and an update to it restates nothing else.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-034}
**NCF-SEM-034** · *Draft*\
A value whose validity differs from that of the rest of a Thing SHOULD be a Thing of its own.
:::

A value with no scheduled update holds until it is changed.
A receiver may still apply a policy of its own, such as showing a position older than a minute as uncertain, or discarding a cached representation it no longer needs.
That is the receiver's presentation or housekeeping, not a change to the Thing: it makes no new version, and the Thing remains at its origin (@sec-origins).

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-035}
**NCF-SEM-035** · *Draft*\
A participant MUST NOT publish as a change to a Thing what is only its own policy for presenting or discarding its cached representation of the Thing.
:::

See [provisional decision 0022](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0022-validity.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How is a value marked as no longer current: by a status the framework defines, or by terms of each vocabulary?
Does every value state when it was measured or observed, as distinct from when its version was made, so that a receiver can judge its age?
:::

Each binding carries these changes in its own terms (Part III).
Each create and update gives the Thing a new version (@sec-versions).

See [provisional decision 0019](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0019-kinds-of-change.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Can a delete be scheduled, as well as an update?
:::

## Versions {#sec-versions}

A Thing changes over its life while keeping its identifier ([NCF-SEM-002](#ncf-sem-002)).
Each create and update gives it a new **version**: its state from that change until the next.
A receiver needs to tell which version of a Thing it holds, and whether that is the latest.

A version is identified by an IRI of its own, which the Thing's owner assigns.
The Thing's IRI refers to the Thing, whichever version is current; a version's IRI refers to that version alone.
Beyond being an IRI, a version's identifier is opaque: an owner forms it as it chooses, and a receiver does not derive it from the Thing's content.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-040}
**NCF-SEM-040** · *Draft*\
Each version of a Thing MUST be identified by an IRI, assigned by the Thing's owner and distinct from the Thing's own IRI.
:::

Only a Thing's origin changes it (@sec-origins), so its versions usually form a single line.
A split origin can branch them while its servers cannot reach one another, and then merges the branches.
Each version but the first names the version it succeeds, and a version that merges branches names the latest version of each.
One version is newer than another if it descends from it; two versions on different branches are concurrent, and neither is newer.
A receiver that holds two versions of a Thing, perhaps received by different routes, tells which is newer by following their predecessors.
When a version was made, for example as `dcterms:modified` [@dcmi-terms], is a hint, not the order.
A merge is a change, so it cancels the changes scheduled against the versions it merges, unless it restates them (@sec-changes).

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-041}
**NCF-SEM-041** · *Draft*\
Each version of a Thing but the first MUST name the version or versions it succeeds.
:::

A scheduled change names the version it produces, as well as the version it was scheduled against (@sec-changes).
A receiver that applies it while out of contact with the owner then holds the same version as the owner, under the same IRI.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-042}
**NCF-SEM-042** · *Draft*\
A scheduled change MUST name the version of the Thing it produces.
:::

A version's IRI is part of the Thing's representation, so that it is the same whichever representation or transport carries the Thing.
A transport's own validators, such as HTTP entity tags [@rfc9110], are the server's choice, and a server can derive them from the version's IRI.
A transport that cannot carry the version, as AIS cannot, gives the receiver an incomplete copy ([NCF-SEM-012](#ncf-sem-012)).

### Earlier versions

The owner of a Thing may keep its earlier versions, each available at its version's IRI.
The version link relations [@rfc5829] link them: `latest-version` to the current version, `predecessor-version` and `successor-version` between versions, and `version-history` to the list of versions.
A version can also refer to the Thing it is a version of, for example with `dcterms:isVersionOf`.
A version's IRI identifies the version whether or not the owner keeps it, as a deleted Thing's IRI does.

A reference to a Thing refers to it whichever version is current.
A reference that needs the Thing as it stood at a given time, such as a record that a vessel was within a notice's zone, names the version by its IRI.

### Short identifiers

A version's IRI, written in full, can be long for a constrained transport.
A representation can write it as a relative IRI, which resolves against the document's base as every IRI in it does [@json-ld11]:
for example, against a notice at `https://example.org/notices/kitkat-zone`, the relative IRI `kitkat-zone/versions/7` resolves to `https://example.org/notices/kitkat-zone/versions/7`.
An owner can also give a version a short IRI, from a URL shortener, that redirects to the version's IRI.
The short IRI is only a locator: the version is identified by the IRI its representation gives itself, not by the address it was reached by.

A JSON-LD document's base, against which its relative IRIs resolve, is by default the location it was finally retrieved from, after any redirects except a 303 See Other [@json-ld11-api].
So that a version's identity never depends on how it was reached, its representation gives its own IRI in full, or sets its base.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-043}
**NCF-SEM-043** · *Draft*\
The representation of a version MUST give the version's IRI as an absolute IRI, or set the base against which its relative IRIs resolve.
:::

See [provisional decision 0020](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0020-versions.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
What does a receiver that holds two concurrent versions of a Thing do until a version that merges them reaches it: keep the one it received last, prefer the one made later, or hold both?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Which terms state the version a representation carries and the version it succeeds: link relations such as `predecessor-version`, DCMI terms, PROV-O's `prov:wasRevisionOf` [@prov-o], or terms of the framework's own?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Does every Thing that ends, such as an expired notice or an organism that has died, remain available at its IRI, ended by an update rather than deleted (@sec-changes), as a notice does ([NCF-VOC-NOT-001](../vocab/notices.qmd#ncf-voc-not-001))?
:::

## Consistency across transports {#sec-consistency}

The framework's central promise is that **information means the same thing everywhere in the system**.
A whale sighting published over IP, relayed over AIS and shown on a chartplotter via NMEA 2000
is the same sighting, with the same meaning, throughout.

Bindings (Part III) keep that promise. Each binding defines how semantic concepts are represented on its transport.

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-010}
**NCF-SEM-010** · *Draft*\
A binding MUST define, for every concept it carries, how that concept is represented on its transport.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-011}
**NCF-SEM-011** · *Draft*\
A representation MUST NOT change the meaning of the information it represents.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-012}
**NCF-SEM-012** · *Draft*\
Where a transport cannot carry all of a Thing, the binding MUST state what is lost and how a receiver can tell that the information is incomplete.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-sem-013}
**NCF-SEM-013** · *Draft*\
A binding MUST preserve, or make recoverable, the identity ([NCF-SEM-001](#ncf-sem-001)) and provenance (@sec-trust-security) of every Thing it carries.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Should there be one **reference representation** (for example JSON-LD [@json-ld11]) that every binding maps to and from?
That would make each binding a single mapping rather than a mapping to every other binding.
See [decision record 0003](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0003-things-as-web-resources.md).
:::
